## What this course is
The foundations of statistics and machine learning: probability, estimation, regression, classification, decision making under uncertainty, model selection, and neural networks. All work is in R.

Given that AI assistants can write the code, fit the models, make the plots, and draft the report, and they can do all of that faster and often better than a first-year graduate student, there is no point in grading you on producing those things. Producing them is not the same as understanding them. You still have to know what your code is doing: what each piece computes, why it is there, and what would break if it were wrong, even when an assistant wrote it.

You will be graded on understanding and judgment. Understanding means you can explain what the analysis is doing, what the numbers mean, and what would change if a modelling choice were different, including when an assistant produced the work. Judgment means choosing what problem is worth solving. Deciding what being wrong costs, and in which direction. Noticing when an analysis is wrong, including when it is your own and including when it came out of a machine. Defending a choice out loud when someone pushes back on it.

I cannot certify either in one sitting. I will ask you to explain the work and then to defend a choice. If you cannot explain what the analysis is doing, I have no reason to trust the choice. That is what class is for.

## Using AI in this course
You are expected to use AI assistants. Getting results from one is fine. What I will not do is take a take-home write-up, script, or report and mark how good it is. That file may have been written by an assistant, and then I would be grading the assistant. Concept checks only test whether a number is right. Everything else that counts is something I can still attach to you: the page your team hands me before you leave, the paper practical, the viva, and the defense.

The rules are short:

1. Use whatever tools you want. There is no approved list.
2. Disclose what you used and for what, in a short appendix on submitted work. No penalty attaches to the disclosure. A team that used an assistant for everything and can defend all of it gets full marks.
3. You are responsible for everything you submit, including the parts you did not write. If you cannot explain it, that is on you.
4. Three assignments require you to use an assistant and then check its work. The code will often run and the numbers will often be right. What you check is whether the assumptions are stated, whether the claims follow from what was computed, and whether the analysis answers the decision it was asked to support. Show how you checked.

The course tutor is a version of an assistant configured for this course: it answers R questions directly, asks you a question back before explaining a concept, and refuses to answer "which model is better?" until you tell it what decision the model supports. Setup is ten minutes, once, in week 1.

## What you will be able to do by December

- Choose and fit an appropriate model for a stated decision, in R, and say why that model and not a simpler or more complex one.
- State what being wrong costs, in both directions, and set thresholds and choose loss functions accordingly rather than by default.
- Quantify uncertainty and say what it means for the decision at hand, rather than reporting an interval and moving on.
- Diagnose a defective analysis from its output: name the defect, point at the evidence, and predict which way the corrected number moves.
- Establish where data came from and whether it is what it claims to be.
- Evaluate a fitted solution against an AI risk framework: who is affected, in which direction errors hurt, and whether the data and the model support the use you are putting them to.
- Defend an analytical choice under live questioning, and change your mind out loud when the questioning is right.

## How a week works
Before class, about 90 minutes on that week's module: read the notes, work the material, and submit the concept check. That 90 minutes does not include project work, which runs on its own clock from week 4. The concept check is a short notebook with three or four auto-graded exercises and one written question. It is low-stakes and its job is to make sure you arrive able to participate. Ask the tutor anything you got stuck on.

In class, one block.

- Live analysis, 25 minutes. I analyse a real, messy dataset on screen with an assistant open beside me, and I hit dead ends on purpose, because watching someone competent be wrong and recover is the part you cannot get from a tutor.
- Studio, 75 to 90 minutes. Your team gets a dataset and a problem, usually an analysis that is already wrong in a way that is not obvious. You work it with whatever tools you like while I move between teams and ask hard questions.
- Critique, 30 to 40 minutes. A team presents; the room takes the analytical choices apart. You will be on both sides of this.

After class. Your team adds one entry to its decision log: a choice you made, the alternative you rejected, and why.

Attendance is not separately graded. There is no studio page in week 7 (the practical) or week 15 (defenses). The practical and both oral checkpoints happen only in class. Missing studio is expensive and cannot be made up by reading.

## Grading

| Component | Weight |
|-----------|-------:|
| Concept checks (13, drop 2) | 15% |
| Studio page, 12 weeks | 15% |
| Viva 10% + project defense 10% | 20% |
| Midterm practical, week 7, closed-AI | 20% |
| Final project | 30% |

Concept checks. Ten notebooks plus three AI-critiques (weeks 5, 9, 13). None in week 7. Auto-graded, due before class, no late credit, lowest two dropped, no individual extensions.

Studio page. On each of the 12 studio weeks, one page before you leave: the finding, the number that proves it, and the decision it changes. Scored on whether you interrogated the result and can say why you chose an approach, not on polish or who talked most. Same rubric each week.

Viva. Five minutes, one on one, weeks 5, 6, 8 or 9. Slot assigned at random and posted in week 4; it happens during studio. Questions go recall, mechanism, justification, then a challenge. Being challenged is not a signal that you are wrong. Changing your mind for a good reason scores well; changing it because I pushed does not. Slots are randomised because a week-9 viva comes with more practice than a week-5 one.

Defense. Eleven minutes per team, Wednesday 9 December, 7:30 to 10:15 pm. Slots posted in week 13, two minutes between teams. The team is scored on how the artifact holds up; each of you is scored on one question directed to you by name, including work you did not personally build.

You are graded on whether you understand the work, including the parts an assistant produced; whether you can justify choices rather than describe them; whether your confidence matches your evidence; and how you handle being pushed. Language fluency is not scored. The rubric is posted in week 1. Week 4 is an ungraded practice round: I viva a few volunteers in front of the room and score them out loud, then you practise on each other.

Practical. Week 7, 60 minutes, on paper, closed-AI. Notes and the textbook are fine; no machine. For each finished analysis you name the one real defect, point at the evidence, and say which way the corrected number moves.

Final project. Teams of 3 to 4, locked in week 4. Proposal due week 7 (a real decision, a stated loss, and a check on where the data came from). Mid-build in studio, week 11. Decision log and a five-minute video due week 14; you watch two assigned teams and name the weakest claim you saw. Artifact due week 15. I do not grade the artifact as a document. I grade the mid-build and the defense. A logistic regression that answers the decision beats a gradient-boosted ensemble that does not. Model sophistication, number of methods tried, and visual polish are not on the rubric. There are no peer evaluations and no contribution percentages.

If the team is not working, tell me by week 9. After that we can reduce your individual scope or reassign you. Waiting until the defense is too late. I will not ask the team to grade each other.

Scores of each component are normalized to be out of 100. I will return component scores as they are graded. Final grades go to Patriot Web. This course uses Mason's graduate regular scale: A\+, A, A\-, B\+, B, B\-, C, F. Cut-offs: 97 (A\+), 93 (A), 90 (A\-), 87 (B+), 82 (B), 79 (B\-), 70 (C). Below 70 is F.

## Computing
All work is in R. Install R and the Jupyter R kernel in week 1; the README is in the course folder.

## Policies

Late work. Concept checks are not accepted late, because we discuss them in class; the two dropped scores cover this. Project components lose credit per day late. Anything in the room (practical, vivas, defense) cannot be made up except through the process below.

Missing an in-class assessment. Tell me before it happens if you possibly can. There is a makeup version of the practical held back for exactly this. Vivas can be rescheduled. Do not simply not appear; that is the only version of this that becomes a real problem.

Accommodations. Students registered with [Disability Services](https://ds.gmu.edu/) should contact me in the first two weeks so we can arrange things properly rather than hastily. This matters more than usual here because 20\% of the grade is oral. Accommodations for oral assessment are routine and include extended time, questions supplied in advance, a written component in place of a spoken one, and a separate quieter room. Ask if you need them.

Academic integrity. Using AI is expected and disclosed, so the usual grey area does not arise. What remains prohibited is what has always been prohibited: submitting someone else's work as your own, fabricating data or results, and misrepresenting what you did. Inventing a number, a source, or an analysis you did not run is the serious offence in this course, and it is the one an assistant makes easiest.

Group work. Team projects are collaborative by design. Concept checks are individual: work with anyone you like, but the submission must be yours and you will be asked about it in the studio.

Recordings. Vivas are audio-recorded if you consent. The recording is so that a score you disagree with is something we can both go back and listen to. If you decline, the viva still happens and I score it from notes; there is then no recording to review later. Only I have access. Files live in a private folder, not in the shared course folder, and I delete them after the grade-appeal window for the term closes.

Project presentations are a required five-minute video, submitted to the course folder. They are visible to me and to the two teams assigned to review yours, not to the rest of the class. If you do not submit the video, that component is missing. Copies are deleted after the grade-appeal window closes.

## University policies
Mason requires every course to make available the [Common Course Policies](https://stearnscenter.gmu.edu/home/gmu-common-course-policies/) (August 2026). They cover academic standards, accommodations for students with disabilities, FERPA and the use of Mason email, and Title IX. That addendum is part of this syllabus. The AI rules in this document are course-specific and sit on top of the university academic standards; they do not replace them. I am a required reporter under the Title IX policy in that addendum. Confidential options are listed there.

## What to do in week 1
Install R and the Jupyter R kernel from the README in the course folder. Set up the course tutor (ten minutes). Read the oral-checkpoint rubric. Knowing what you will be asked in the viva (your slot is in week 5, 6, 8 or 9) changes how you read the weeks before it. Start noticing datasets you have access to through work, research, or an organisation you are part of. The strongest projects use data the team had to negotiate for or assemble. The weakest use a clean file downloaded from a competition site. You will be choosing in week 7 and it is much easier if you start looking now.

## Two things worth saying plainly
The most uncomfortable part of this course is being asked "why?" and not having an answer, in a room, out loud, while people wait. That happens to everyone here, including me. The ungraded practice viva in week 4 is there so the first time is not the graded one.

You will encounter AI-produced work you do not initially understand. Your responsibility is to interrogate it before submitting and defending it. I would rather that happen here than at work.
